result: E-cadherin and P-cadherin show distinct expression patterns in the hair follicle bulge, with E-cadherin strongly expressed at the stem cell-niche interface and P-cadherin specifically concentrated at stem cell-stem cell junctions. P-cadherin transcript and protein levels in stem cells are substantially higher than E-cadherin.
evaluation: Claims C20-C23 are well-supported by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 1A), RNA-seq data showing ~20X higher Cdh3 transcripts in stem cells vs niche cells (C22), and ELISA quantification showing higher P-cadherin than E-cadherin protein levels in FACS-purified stem cells (C23, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). The complementary expression pattern is clearly demonstrated.

result: P-cadherin (Cdh3) null mice display normal hair coat, hair cycle, and E-cadherin expression throughout the bulge, with hair germ cells proliferating normally during early anagen.
evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D showing normal hair coat appearance, maintained E-cadherin expression at all cell-cell junctions, and EdU incorporation in hair germ during early anagen. This demonstrates functional redundancy between cadherins as cited (Tinkle et al., 2008).

result: Conditional ablation of Cdh1 in the bulge results in efficient E-cadherin depletion throughout the bulge by 3 weeks post-tamoxifen. Cdh1-null stem cells maintain adherens junctions at stem cell-stem cell borders through compensatory P-cadherin upregulation, but the inner bulge layer lacks both cadherins and adherens junctions, leaving the stem cell-niche interface devoid of adherens junctions.
evaluation: Claims C27-C34 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: immunofluorescence showing E-cadherin depletion (Figure 1B), maintained P-cadherin at stem cell-stem cell junctions (Figure 1C), immunoblot quantification showing elevated P-cadherin in Cdh1-null stem cells (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-D), and loss of p120-catenin at the stem cell-niche interface (Figure 1C). The mechanistic inference about AJ loss at the interface (C31) is sound given the requirement for homophilic cadherin binding.

result: Adherens junctions form an intercellular F-actin network across epithelial sheets. In wild-type hair follicles, F-actin organization is particularly robust in the inner bulge, but becomes markedly perturbed throughout the inner bulge in the absence of E-cadherin.
evaluation: Claims C35-C37 are supported by established knowledge about AJ-actin networks (citations provided), phalloidin staining showing robust F-actin in WT inner bulge, and quantification demonstrating significant disruption in Cdh1 cKO (Figure 1E). The data clearly show the structural consequences of E-cadherin loss.

result: Tight junction proteins remain largely intact in CD34+ stem cells but are disrupted in niche cells of the Cdh1-null bulge. Lucifer yellow dye penetrates the E-cadherin-deficient inner bulge layer, indicating loss of tight junction integrity and barrier function.
evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by immunofluorescence and immunoblot data showing disrupted tight junction proteins in the niche (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E) and functional barrier assay demonstrating dye penetration in Cdh1 cKO (Figure 1G). This provides both molecular and functional evidence of barrier breach.

result: Despite loss of E-cadherin, niche cells are not lost from the bulge. Desmosomes remain present in normal morphology, numbers and localization, intercellular membranes at the niche-stem cell interface remain sealed, and the inner bulge layer remains adhered to the club hair via half-desmosomal structures.
evaluation: Claims C40-C42 are supported by electron microscopy and immunofluorescence data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C) showing maintained desmosomal structures and sealed membranes. This demonstrates that while AJs and tight junctions are compromised, desmosomes provide sufficient adhesion to maintain tissue architecture.

result: Upon homozygous Cdh1 ablation, telogen-phase bulge stem cells begin proliferating, in striking contrast to normal hair cycle dynamics where proliferation initiates first in the hair germ. This telogen-phase proliferation is neither preceded nor accompanied by hair germ proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are well-supported by EdU incorporation data and quantification (Figure 2A) showing proliferation specifically in the bulge but not hair germ of Cdh1 cKO mice during telogen, contrasting with normal hair cycle progression in controls. This represents a major deviation from normal stem cell behavior.

result: Cdh1 cKO hair follicles spend longer in telogen before entering anagen. Telogen-phase stem cell proliferation produces additional bulge layers rather than launching a new hair cycle. Daughter cells retain stem cell identity (CD34+, LHX2+, TCF4+, SOX9+), resulting in significant expansion of stem cell numbers within the Cdh1-null bulge.
evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by hair cycle analysis showing delayed anagen entry (Figure 2B), histology showing hyperthickened bulge (Figure 2C), immunofluorescence confirming stem cell marker expression (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and quantification showing significant increase in CD34+ cell numbers (Figure 2D). This demonstrates repurposing of proliferation from regeneration to niche reinforcement.

result: Despite increased proliferation in telogen, Cdh1-null HF stem cells remain sensitive to hair cycle cues and return to quiescence in subsequent anagen and telogen, suggesting normal hair cycling cues remain in place.
evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by EdU incorporation data showing stem cells return to quiescence in subsequent hair cycles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). The inference that normal cues remain (C51) is reasonable given the observed responsiveness to hair cycle signals.

result: P-cadherin overexpression in skin epithelium has no significant effect on stem cell proliferation. Selective ablation of Cdh1 in bulge stem cells alone does not cause ectopic proliferation or bulge expansion, pointing to perturbations within the niche as the source of the proliferative stimulus.
evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by EdU incorporation data showing no proliferation with P-cadherin overexpression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) or with stem cell-specific Cdh1 ablation (Figure 2F). The inference that niche perturbations drive proliferation (C54) is well-supported by these negative controls.

result: In Krt15CrePGR-activated mice, bulge stem cells proliferate and expand concomitant with E-cadherin loss in the inner bulge during subsequent hair cycles. Selective Cdh1 ablation in the inner bulge niche alone is sufficient to elicit bulge hyperthickening even when stem cells are wild-type, suggesting bulge stem cell proliferation relies on the direct interface with the defective niche.
evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by temporal analysis showing proliferation correlates with inner bulge Cdh1 loss (Figure 2G), and niche-specific ablation experiments showing WT stem cells proliferate adjacent to Cdh1-null niche (Figure 2H). The inference about interface dependence (C57) is well-supported by the collective genetic dissection experiments.

result: Cdh1 cKO hair follicles are infiltrated with both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria as shown by Gram staining and 16S rRNA FISH, highlighting the importance of a healthy inner bulge niche in protecting stem cells and skin against microbial infiltration.
evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by Gram staining showing both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (Figure 3A) and 16S rRNA FISH with quantification (Figure 3B). The inference about niche barrier function (C59) is reasonable given the observed bacterial infiltration following barrier breach.

result: Antibiotics treatment efficiently depletes microbes from the skin as judged by 16S rRNA FISH. Despite efficient microbial clearing, the Cdh1 cKO bulge remains proliferative and hyper-thickened, ruling out bacteria as the instigating factor in stem cell proliferation when the niche barrier is breached.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are well-supported by 16S rRNA FISH quantification showing bacterial depletion (Figure 3B) and EdU incorporation data showing persistent proliferation and hyperthickening despite antibiotics treatment (Figure 3C). This is a critical control demonstrating bacteria are not required for the proliferative response.

result: CD45+ immune cells selectively surround the Cdh1-null bulge with a marked and statistically significant increase within a 25 μm radius compared to controls. Immune cell accumulation begins by day 23 post-Cdh1 ablation, before the increase in bacterial load and shift to triple-layered bulge architecture.
evaluation: Claims C63-C65 are supported by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry (Figure 4A), quantification showing significant increase in CD45+ cells near the bulge (Figure 4C), and temporal analysis showing immune cell accumulation precedes bacterial increase and architectural changes (Figure 4B). This temporal sequence is important for establishing causality.

result: Immune cells are still recruited to the breached niche when bacteria are depleted with antibiotics. Selective Cdh1 ablation from stem cells alone does not recruit immune cells until the inner bulge becomes Cdh1-null in subsequent cycles. Selective Cdh1 ablation in the inner bulge alone elicits robust immune response.
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by immunofluorescence and quantification showing immune recruitment persists with antibiotics (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), no recruitment with stem cell-specific ablation until niche is affected (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C), and robust response with niche-specific ablation (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). This genetic dissection clearly demonstrates the niche is the source of immune recruitment signals.

result: The immune response to the breached niche goes beyond normal surveillance, with clear compositional differences from normal resident immune patterns. Notable increases include CD3+ T cells, CD11b+ myeloid cells, MHCII+ CD11c+ dendritic cells, and αβ T cells (particularly FOXP3+ Tregs). Treg numbers surrounding the bulge are markedly higher than normal skin resident populations.
evaluation: Claims C69-C77 are well-supported by comprehensive immunofluorescence and flow cytometry analysis (Figure 4D-F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G) with statistical quantification. The characterization of immune cell types is rigorous, using multiple markers to define populations (e.g., DCs as MHCII+ CD11c+ CD64-/low). The variability in macrophage numbers (C73) is appropriately noted as not statistically significant.

result: RNA-seq reveals distinct transcriptional responses in stem cells versus niche cells from Cdh1-null bulge. The inner bulge upregulates cell adhesion, proteoglycans and cytoskeletal genes while downregulating metabolism. Stem cells upregulate cell cycle and immune signaling/response genes. Proliferative WT stem cells in normal anagen do not show immune pathway gene expression. PCA highlights marked distinctions between proliferative stem cells in normal tissue growth versus those repurposed for niche repair.
evaluation: Claims C78-C82 are strongly supported by comprehensive RNA-seq analysis with KEGG pathway enrichment (Figure 5A-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-F), comparison to WT anagen stem cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), and PCA (Figure 5E). The transcriptomic data clearly demonstrate distinct responses in different cell populations and contexts. Sample sizes (n=2-4 biological replicates) are adequate for RNA-seq.

result: Most immune signaling genes in the breached niche signature are more highly expressed by stem cells than niche cells. Ccl1 and Ccl2 are the top two most highly upregulated genes in stem cells (184X, 38X fold-change) and are established chemokines for dendritic cells and macrophages. These genes remain robustly expressed even when microbial infiltration is repressed, suggesting stem cells recruit immune cells in direct response to the damaged niche rather than bacteria.
evaluation: Claims C83-C87 are well-supported by RNA-seq data showing differential expression between cell types (Figure 5F-G), high fold-changes for Ccl1/Ccl2 (Figure 5C), established knowledge about these chemokines (citations provided), and qRT-PCR showing maintained expression with antibiotics treatment (Figure 5H). The inference about direct niche response (C87) is strongly supported by the antibiotics control.

result: Cdh1-null HF stem cells retain elevated Ccl2 in culture and significantly increase chemotaxis of bone marrow-derived dendritic cells in transwell assays. This increased chemotaxis is abolished using CCR2-null DCs. Macrophage migration shows a similar trend but is highly variable and not statistically significant. CCR8 blocking antibody reduces chemotactic response, and combined CCR2/CCR8 blocking further reduces migration. These findings indicate HF stem cells experiencing barrier breach can activate chemokines and directly recruit immune cells.
evaluation: Claims C88-C94 are well-supported by qRT-PCR from cultured cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H), transwell migration assays with multiple controls including CCR2-null cells and CCR8 blocking antibody (Figure 5I-J). The statistical analysis appropriately notes the variability in macrophage responses (C91). The mechanistic inference (C92, C94) is strongly supported by the receptor blocking experiments. Sample size (n=3) is adequate for in vitro assays.

result: Dexamethasone effectively blocks immune infiltration around the breached niche barrier. Dex-treated Cdh1 cKO HFs display normal bulge architecture, with abolished telogen-phase proliferation and stem cell expansion. Enhanced BMP-signaling effector pSMAD1 is observed in Dex-treated Cdh1 cKO stem cells.
evaluation: Claims C95-C98 are well-supported by immunofluorescence and quantification showing blocked immune infiltration (Figure 6A), normal bulge architecture (Figure 6B), abolished proliferation and stem cell expansion (Figure 6B), and enhanced pSMAD1 (Figure 6B). This demonstrates immune cells are required for the proliferative response. The experimental design appropriately starts Dex treatment after Cdh1 ablation but before immune recruitment.

result: BMP6 is still expressed by Cdh1-null inner bulge cells, and HF stem cells in the breached niche still express BMP target genes (Nfatc1, Foxc1). Dexamethasone alone does not inhibit HF stem cell proliferation directly in vitro. Bacteria remain present in immunosuppressed skin, indicating microbial infiltration arises from loss of junctional integrity rather than architectural disturbances from proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C99-C103 are supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), in vitro growth curves showing no direct Dex effect (Figure 6B), and 16S rRNA FISH showing persistent bacteria (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). The inference about junctional integrity (C103) is reasonable given bacteria persist when proliferation is blocked.

result: Dendritic cells and Tregs are closely associated when surrounding the breached niche. Dex treatment markedly blocks their infiltration into the Cdh1-null bulge niche. The immunosuppressive effects appear specific for immune infiltration to the bulge, as immune cells elsewhere in the skin remain during treatment.
evaluation: Claims C104-C106 are supported by immunofluorescence showing DC-Treg co-localization and blocked infiltration with Dex (Figure 6C). The specificity observation (C106) is important for demonstrating the response is localized to the site of barrier breach.

result: In co-culture assays, dendritic cells show no appreciable effect on HF stem cell proliferation, while Tregs are particularly robust in soliciting a proliferative response.
evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are supported by in vitro co-culture assay data (Figure 6D). However, the assay uses compartmentalized cultures (transwell) so effects are mediated by secreted factors. The sample size (n=3 in triplicate) is adequate for in vitro assays. This identifies Tregs as a key proliferative stimulus.

result: Most canonical NOTCH target genes are very lowly expressed in normal telogen HF stem cells and are not elevated appreciably when the niche barrier is altered and swarmed with Tregs. The authors surmise Tregs' proliferative effects are more likely rooted in amphiregulin and/or keratinocyte growth factor.
evaluation: Claims C109-C110 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B) showing low NOTCH target gene expression. However, C111 is explicitly labeled as speculation by the authors and is not directly tested. While the speculation is reasonable based on known Treg functions (citations provided), it remains unvalidated. Additional experiments would be needed to confirm the mechanism.

result: RNA-seq of Dex-treated Cdh1-null versus control stem cells reveals 509 upregulated genes, of which 392 (77%) are also upregulated in non-treated counterparts. Despite stem cells being non-proliferative under Dex, the top KEGG pathway among these 392 genes is cell cycle. Cell cycle transcripts are significantly upregulated in Cdh1-null stem cells independent of both Dex treatment and Cdh1 loss in the stem cells themselves.
evaluation: Claims C112-C115 are well-supported by RNA-seq analysis with Venn diagram (Figure 7A), KEGG pathway analysis (Figure 7B), and gene expression quantification (Figure 7C). This demonstrates that niche defects alone are sufficient to elevate cell cycle genes, but proliferation requires additional signals from immune cells. The experimental design appropriately dissects these contributions.

result: Many immune response genes persist in HF stem cells in a breached niche even under immunosuppressive conditions. The necessary threshold level of cell cycle transcripts for proliferation is contributed in part by the Cdh1-null niche and in part by the ability of stem cells to recruit immune cells.
evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are supported by gene expression data showing persistent immune gene expression with Dex (Figure 7D). The inference about threshold contributions (C117) is reasonable given the observation that cell cycle genes are elevated but insufficient for proliferation without immune cells.

result: Many immune response transcripts remaining elevated in Dex-treated cKO stem cells are putative NFkB target genes. Previous work showed p120-catenin ablation elevates IKK activity, resulting in IkBα phosphorylation and NFkB nuclear release. NFkB shows nuclear localization in telogen-phase Cdh1-null HF stem cells. Dexamethasone has only partial effect on NFkB signaling under conditions of enhanced IkBα phosphorylation. The authors propose a mechanism where barrier breach and reduced adherens junctions impact NFkB activity, altering the transcriptional landscape to promote immune recruitment and reduce proliferation threshold.
evaluation: Claims C118-C121 are supported by gene expression data (Figure 7E), citation to previous work on p120-catenin/NFkB (Perez-Moreno et al., 2006), immunofluorescence showing nuclear NFkB (Figure 7F), and gene expression showing partial Dex effect (Figure 7E). The mechanistic model (C122) is a reasonable inference based on the collective data, though the authors appropriately note further details are beyond the scope of the study. The reduced p120 levels at the stem cell-niche interface (Figure 1C-D) support the proposed mechanism.

result: When junctional perturbations disrupt niche barrier function, adjacent stem cells dramatically change their transcriptome independent of bacterial invasion, become capable of directly signaling to and recruiting immune cells, elevate cell cycle transcripts reducing their quiescence threshold, and selectively proliferate within the microenvironment of immune distress cues. Rather than mobilizing for tissue regeneration, these proliferative stem cells remain within their niche to contain the breach, patching the barrier, stoking immune response, and restoring niche integrity.
evaluation: This result synthesizes the major findings of the study. Claims C3-C7 are supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence detailed in previous result groups: RNA-seq showing transcriptional changes independent of bacteria (antibiotics controls), transwell assays demonstrating direct immune cell recruitment, RNA-seq showing cell cycle gene upregulation, EdU incorporation showing proliferation dependent on immune cells, and immunofluorescence showing stem cells remain CD34+ within the bulge with delayed anagen entry. Claim C8 is an interpretive synthesis that is reasonable given the observed expansion of stem cell layers with intact AJs, continued immune signaling, and immune cell recruitment, though the authors acknowledge this is inference rather than direct demonstration of barrier repair.

result: The inner bulge provides a barrier protecting stem cells from microbial invasion. Stem cells co-express P- and E-cadherin, protecting them when E-cadherin is downregulated. Stem cells can sense barrier breach independent of bacteria or immune cells, likely through inability to form adherens junctions with Cdh1-null niche neighbors. Adherens junctions act as signaling centers integrating proliferation, polarity and cytoskeleton, and serve as regulators of inflammatory sensors.
evaluation: Claims C123-C128 represent key conclusions of the study. C123 is supported by bacterial infiltration data (Figure 3). C124 is supported by cadherin compensation data (Figure 1). C125 is supported by antibiotics and Dex experiments showing transcriptional changes persist. C126 is reasonable speculation given the loss of AJs at the stem cell-niche interface. C127 is established knowledge (citations provided). C128 is a conclusion supported by the current findings and previous work (citation provided).

result: Stem cells facing a breached niche barrier trigger a distress transcriptional program that occurs even with antibiotics or immunosuppression and differs strikingly from the niche cell response. Stem cells are capable of altering their transcriptional program in response to microenvironmental perturbations and can adjust their behavior by directly recruiting immune cells.
evaluation: Claims C129-C130 are supported by RNA-seq data from multiple conditions showing distinct responses in stem cells vs niche cells (Figure 5). Claims C133-C134 represent major findings supported by RNA-seq and functional assays (transwell migration, in vivo immune profiling). This demonstrates a previously unrecognized capability of stem cells.

result: Proliferative effects of Tregs on HF stem cells can be direct. In homeostasis and hair plucking, stem cells proliferate to launch hair growth, while with barrier breach they contain damage. This difference likely resides in different immune cell-derived factors under different conditions. The communication between stem cells and immune cells in barrier breach is more robust and diverse than in normal cycling or injury. Stem cells sense and respond to their environment, recruiting distinct immune repertoires to receive new instructions that channel their efforts in new directions, enabling immune cells to repurpose stem cells from hair growth to barrier repair.
evaluation: Claim C141 is supported by co-culture data (Figure 6D). Claims C142-C147 represent interpretive conclusions synthesizing the findings. C142 is supported by comparison to previous studies (citations provided). C143 is reasonable speculation based on known immune cell functions (citations provided). C144 is supported by the comprehensive transcriptomic and functional data. C145-C147 are interpretive conclusions that are well-supported by the collective evidence showing repurposing of proliferation from regeneration to barrier reinforcement.

result: Diversion of HF stem cells from regeneration adds AJ-competent cell layers to reinforce the damaged bulge and amplifies local production of distress signals. This communication network appears aimed at patching the breached barrier and limiting tissue damage from chronic inflammation. The hyperthickening phenotype is locally restricted to the site of barrier breach.
evaluation: Claims C148-C149 are interpretations supported by the observed expansion of stem cells with intact AJs and upregulation of immune signaling genes. C150 is a reasonable interpretation of the overall findings. C151 is supported by histology and immunofluorescence showing changes localized to the bulge (Figure 8, Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).

result: In the genetic Cdh1-null model, stem cell efforts to patch the barrier are futile as evidenced by persistent bacterial infiltration. Genetic disorders with breached barriers show stem cell hyperproliferation unable to repair the barrier. In epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, healthy stem cells maintain single proliferative layer while expanding defective differentiated layers. Cdh1-null HF stem cells cannot directly generate terminally differentiated barrier cells and instead generate multiple stem cell layers. These responses likely reflect a general, evolutionarily conserved mechanism for stem cells to respond to barrier defects.
evaluation: Claim C152 is supported by persistent bacterial infiltration data (Figure 3). C153 is general knowledge. C154 is established knowledge about epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (citation provided). C155 is supported by the observed expansion of CD34+ stem cell layers and citation to previous work on HF lineage. C156 is reasonable speculation based on comparison of different barrier breach models, though it remains speculative without direct evolutionary evidence.

result: Studies in Drosophila established E-cadherin's role in adhering germline stem cells to their niche. The increased HF stem cell proliferation in response to reduced adherens junctions could reflect direct response to the perturbed interface. Immune suppression keeps ectopic proliferation largely in check, exposing additional complexity in proliferative control not seen in invertebrate systems.
evaluation: Claim C157 is established knowledge (citations provided). C158 is reasonable speculation based on the observed correlation. C159 is a well-supported conclusion based on the Dex experiments showing proliferation depends on immune cells (Figure 6). This represents a key distinction from invertebrate stem cell systems.

result: Stem cells displaying hyperproliferative response can be wild-type and depend on their border with damaged niche neighbors. Despite immune response being critical for proliferation, telogen-phase stem cells in damaged niche maintain a cell proliferation transcriptome even when immune response is repressed, paralleling their natural proliferative state. In early anagen, stimulatory factors outweigh quiescence factors, but in damaged telogen niche, quiescence factors remain high and reduced AJs plus elevated cell cycle genes are insufficient alone. The proliferative trigger becomes contingent on immune distress signals upon niche barrier failure.
evaluation: Claim C163 is supported by experiments showing WT stem cells proliferate adjacent to Cdh1-null niche (Figure 2H). C164-C165 are supported by RNA-seq from Dex-treated samples (Figure 7). C166 is established knowledge. C167 is supported by the observation that Dex-treated stem cells don't proliferate despite elevated cell cycle genes and maintained BMP signaling. C168 is a well-supported mechanistic conclusion integrating the findings.

result: Stem cells respond to damaged niche by altering gene expression to prime for proliferation and recruit immune cells. Immune cells bestow growth factors and cytokines on the niche. Tregs may limit tissue damage from inflammation. Primed stem cells have reduced proliferation threshold and selectively respond to recruited immune cells while other cells remain quiescent. This selective self-renewal sustains immune response and reinforces the barrier with cells having intact junctions. The findings explain pathological conditions where perturbations in terminally differentiating cells manifest in healthy stem/progenitor cells.
evaluation: Claims C169-C173 represent the integrated mechanistic model supported by the collective findings. C169 is supported by RNA-seq data. C170 is a reasonable inference based on the requirement for immune cells and known immune cell functions. C171 is speculation based on known Treg functions and their observed accumulation. C172 is supported by the observation that only bulge stem cells, not hair germ, proliferate. C173 is supported by the observed expansion of stem cells with intact AJs and continued immune signaling. C174 is a broader implication that is reasonable given the findings.
